summary: Degrade and priority inheritance are unreconciled; PriorityInheritingLock restores a pre-boost priority on unlock so a degrade applied to a boosted holder is silently undone, and degrading a boosted task discards a boost a waiter depends on. Tcb now holds base_priority (what wcet degrade lowers) and inherited_priority (what lock boost raises), and the priority everything SCHEDULES on is derived as their max on demand, so there is no stored decision left for a second writer to invalidate. The writers are separated by name -- set_base_priority for wcet, inherit_priority and release_inheritance for lock -- and neither can reach the other field. Both orderings now compose: a degrade taken while boosted survives the unlock (the task lands on its floor, not its pre-boost priority) and a degrade applied to a boosted holder does not disturb the boost, so the waiter is not starved by an unrelated overrun. summary: GICC_PMR's implemented priority width was compiled in, not discovered, and the first silicon disproved it: gic.rs declares PRIORITY_MASK_ALL = 0xF8 with the comment "GIC-400 implements 32 priority levels, so the low three bits read as zero", writes it, and refuses routing unless readback & 0xF8 == 0xF8. BOARD VERDICT 5 read back 0xF0, so the virtual-timer PPI was refused as MaskNotHeld(0xF0) and STORY-P1-07-04 criterion 1 (tick count, rmin/rmax) has no evidence. 0xF0 is conformant: GICv2 leaves unimplemented low-order priority bits RAZ/WI with the implemented bits contiguous from bit 7 down, so 0xF0 means BCM2712 implements four priority bits (16 levels), the architectural minimum, not five. The code refused a conforming device. Same class as the three ethernet cures (outbound window, endpoint BARs, inbound windows): device state that must be read, not assumed. Fixing it as 0xF8 -> 0xF0 is barred - that substitutes one board's measured value for another guess and violates the no-bench-tuned-constants rule
origin: BOARD VERDICT 5 (TinyOS measure boot 2026-08-04), TOS64-TICK/1 REFUSED=GICC-PMR READBACK=000000F0
owner_path: Discover the width instead of asserting it: write all ones to GICC_PMR and take the readback as the widest legal open mask for that implementation; gate on conformance of shape (implemented bits a contiguous run ending at bit 7, at least four of them per GICv2) rather than equality against a constant; carry the discovered mask into the tick evidence line so the width is recorded per board rather than assumed per family; re-run the measure boot and read a live TOS64-TICK/1 with its ratio bounds

summary: Interrupt masking around the measurement region had no scope, and the defect was unreachable-by-construction rather than intermittent. fixture_measure_arm64 called hal_arm64::boot::mask_interrupts() with the recorded reasoning that "masking is one-way here ... the tick line having accumulated its pre-fixture intervals is itself evidence"; hal_arm64::boot::unmask_interrupts() existed with NO callers anywhere in the tree. The premise is false on silicon: the only window the tick can fire in is between the daifclr after GIC bring-up and the fixture's mask, containing just the 64-sample conformance run and the PMU probe, and BOARD VERDICT 6 measured what it admits - TOS64-TICK/1 COUNT=1. One tick is one timestamp is ZERO intervals, and ratio_bounds_per_mille returns None below two intervals by design, so STORY-P1-07-04 criterion 1 (a tick verified by ratio) could never be satisfied on any board however many times it was booted. Every layer was individually correct; the ordering was the defect and no host test owned it. Found only because criterion 1 was chased onto hardware after LE-69 cleared the GIC refusal that had been masking it

summary: The boot epoch STORY-P1-10-04 puts in every spoor frame is a distinguisher, not an identifier. It is derived from CNTVCT_EL0 at kernel entry, so it differs between boots only because firmware timing differs between boots -- there is no persistent store and no RTC on the Pi 5 path to derive anything stronger from. Two boots whose firmware happened to take the same number of counter ticks to reach the kernel produce the same epoch and a host reads them as one boot. A host can therefore conclude "this is a different boot" with high probability and can never conclude "this is boot number N" or "I missed exactly two boots", and the field must never be documented as though it could MEASURED 2026-08-05 and it is thinner than this row assumed: three consecutive boots of fd966f7514e4 produced epochs 0x049F8B28, 0x04B328BC and 0x04B32825. The last two differ by 0x97 = 151 counter ticks, which at 54 MHz is 2.8 MICROSECONDS - two power cycles put the kernel entry point within three microseconds of the same counter reading, so only the low byte of the epoch moved. The first pair differ by ~1.28M ticks (~23 ms), so the variation is not uniform, but a pair landing 151 ticks apart makes collision a plausible event rather than a theoretical one and a collision reads as 'same boot' to every host. BOARD VERDICTS 11-13 still stand - those epochs did differ and were read as different - so this bounds the field's future use rather than retracting any result: sound as a bench-session change detector, never an identifier, and any host or document treating it as one is wrong by measurement now and not merely by caution
owner_path: BCM2712 has a hardware RNG (rng200) that would make the epoch a genuine nonce, and firmware-persisted state would make it a genuine counter; both are their own device bring-up and neither is in FEAT-P1-10. Until one exists, every document and every host tool states the epoch as a change detector rather than as a boot number

summary: TinyOS drives the Pi 5 with no thermal awareness of any kind: it never reads the SoC temperature sensor, has no throttle path, and does not program RP1 PWM, so the fan connector is dead on every TinyOS boot. Observed by the owner during the STORY-P1-10-04 board session on 2026-08-05 - the fan spins immediately under Pi OS (Linux binds pwm-fan to a thermal zone and sets the duty cycle from the measured temperature) and never spins under TinyOS. This is not a defect in any Story; it is an absence nothing has ever owned. It touches rule 1 of agent.md - safety before security before correctness before performance - and the honest statement of the current position is that thermal management on this board is entirely the firmware's, TinyOS neither cooperates with it nor knows whether it is happening. Board sessions to date are 30-90 second captures and nothing about them is evidence for sustained operation; hand-2026-08-04/05A recorded the board left "powered, beaconing" between sessions, which is the shape of unattended continuous running that this row argues against until the gap is closed CALIBRATION ROUTE CLOSED 2026-08-05: the raw AVS datum cannot be read under Pi OS at all. /dev/mem mmap at 0x107d542000 returns EINVAL under STRICT_DEVMEM, and the only other route - the syscon debugfs regmap at /sys/kernel/debug/regmap/dummy-avs-monitor@0x000000107d542000/registers - RESET THE BOARD when read, because the region is 0xf0000 bytes and the kernel materialises ~983000 register reads before any truncation applies (SSH dropped mid-read; /proc/uptime read 110 s afterwards). Do not repeat it. So the two-point fit this row asked for is not obtainable from Linux on this card, and the honest position is PUBLISHED CONSTANTS CORROBORATED ON THIS BOARD rather than independently derived: BOARD VERDICT 14 shows the raw datum falling monotonically 758->746 as the die warms with validity bit 16 set throughout, deriving 40.9->46.7 C from cold against 38.05 C measured under Pi OS at idle. That is corroboration and is not a calibration; Ti64Dink keeps the unverified marker until a route to the raw value exists - a kernel module, a different kernel config, or reading it from TinyOS at a temperature Linux independently reports

owner_path: Two separable pieces, sensing before actuation. First, read the temperature: transcribe the BCM2712 thermal sensor from the Pi OS ground truth already captured in this file and put the reading on the spoor stream as its own rung, so the board can say how hot it is before anything tries to act on it. Second, drive the fan from that reading through RP1 PWM - derived from the measured temperature and never a hardcoded duty cycle, the discipline LE-69 was closed under. Until the first piece exists, the operational rule is that the board is powered for a run and powered down after it, and no document claims anything about sustained thermal behaviour

summary: The TOS64-MEAS/2 measurement envelope rides the wire as a CYCLING TEXT TRANSCRIPT with none of the guarantees the spoor channel next to it has, and the gap is structural rather than cosmetic. A spoor frame carries a 64-bit sequence, a boot epoch, a record count and a flags word, so loss is an exact count, boots are distinguishable, order is guaranteed and the boot prologue is retained for a late listener. A transcript line carries NOTHING - no sequence, no epoch, no framing - because it predates the spoor substrate and was built as FEAT-P1-09/STORY-P1-07-06 bring-up evidence. Three consequences, all observed on 2026-08-05: a capture starting mid-cycle sees a ROTATION of the envelope rather than the envelope, and xtask parse-meas rightly refuses it (no BEGIN before the first record); a lost line is INVISIBLE because there is no gap accounting on this channel; and a capture spanning a reboot would interleave two boots envelopes with nothing to tell them apart. Ti64Dink recovers order today by filtering to TOS64-MEAS/2 lines and rotating so BEGIN is first, which is exact - but it rests on an ASSUMPTION ABOUT THE EMITTER (that BEGIN is line 0 of the cycle) rather than on a property of the wire, which is precisely the class of assumption LE-69, LE-71 and LE-74 were each raised over

summary: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` reports success-or-failure for the workspace but does NOT lint the whole workspace when any crate fails to compile: cargo stops at the first failure and every package after it goes unlinted, silently. On this Windows bench `kernel`s [[bin]] names `hal_x86_64` items gated cfg(not(windows)) so it cannot compile at all, which means the workspace run has been dying at `kernel` and never reaching the crates after it -- for the entire life of the bench. Proved by an `unused import: crate::board` in hal-arm64/src/thermal.rs that passed every local gate and was caught only by CI on Linux (run 31012173030, the first red push since LE-72 closed). This is LE-64s Windows-host-blindness class in a new form: LE-64 and LE-72 are both about code the host cannot COMPILE, and this is about code the host silently never LINTS because something earlier failed. The lesson generalises past clippy -- any batch command that stops on first failure reports on a prefix of its subject while appearing to report on all of it
origin: CI run 31012173030 red on push db94d98, 2026-08-05; local cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets green because it never reached hal-arm64
owner_path: Closed by `cargo run -p xtask -- check-lints`: one clippy invocation PER PACKAGE so a failure reports itself instead of hiding the next crate, every package attempted even after one fails, and all failures reported together so a session sees them in one run rather than one push at a time. Scoped to --lib --tests (plus --all-targets for the bin-only xtask) because the cfg(not(windows)) fixture bins in exec/shell/kernel can never build here and a gate that always fails is a gate nobody runs -- LE-72s own lesson applied to itself; those bins stay covered by CIs Linux workspace run. On its first run it found a second real lint (a constant-value assertion in thermal.rs) that the workspace run had never reached
